# Kukkurajātaka (Ja 22)

**ID:** Ja 22
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Dog

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kukkurajātaka* (Ja 22) is a canonical birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection (PTS Ja I 175–178) [Fausböll 1877; Lang 2003]. According to the commentary's frame story, the Buddha narrated the tale while residing at Jetavana to illustrate acting for the welfare of one's kinsfolk (*ñātatthacariyā*), a theme connected to the *Bhaddasālajātaka* of the Twelfth Book [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as the leader of a pack of dogs in Bārāṇasī during the reign of King Brahmadatta [Fausböll 1877; UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. After the leather straps and carriage harnesses of the royal chariot are gnawed overnight, the king orders the indiscriminate killing of all dogs in the city, exempting only his own well-bred palace hounds [UNDV Conference Volume 2009; Fenn 1994]. The Bodhisatta intervenes, demonstrates that the palace dogs were the true culprits, and challenges the ruler's partiality in slaughtering vulnerable stray dogs (*dubbala*) while protecting the privileged [Fenn 1994; UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. The text's canonical verse begins: *Ye kukkurā rājakulasmi vaddhā...* ("The dogs that in the royal palace grow...") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].

Scholars highlight the narrative as an ethical and socio-political critique regarding justice, nonviolence (*ahiṃsā*), and the religio-political obligations of kingship to protect all subjects impartially [Fenn 1994; Lang 2003]. An abbreviated version of the *Kukkurajātaka* is cited by Candrakīrti in his commentary on Āryadeva's *Catuḥśataka*, where the Bodhisatta dog instructs the monarch in Buddhist virtues and secures a decree protecting the lives of all creatures in the realm [Lang 1983; Lang 2003]. The story is also cataloged across Southeast Asian manuscript collections and regional Jātaka compilations [Skilling].

Curated records and algorithmic analyses report no internal Pali text reuse or cross-language matches exceeding significant threshold scores [DharmaNexus; SuttaCentral]. However, Candrakīrti's *Catuḥśatakaṭīkā* preserves an explicit Sanskrit parallel and commentary citation [Lang 1983; Lang 2003]. English translations include a rendering by Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
